nameStory: The "club" in Club Pincushion comes from its distinctive sporophytes (spore capsules) that stand up like tiny clubs from the moss cushions. Like other pincushion mosses, it forms dense, rounded cushions that look just like the fabric pincushions your grandmother might have used for sewing, complete with little "pins" sticking out.
description: Club Pincushion is a small moss that forms tight, rounded cushions on tree bark, looking like miniature green pincushions dotting the trunk. Each cushion is typically only about half an inch across, made up of densely packed tiny stems with overlapping leaves. When conditions are right, small reddish-brown capsules on short stalks poke up from the cushions like pins in a pincushion.

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms small, dense, rounded cushions on tree bark that feel firm and springy to the touch, like tiny natural pincushions

idTips.label: Sporophytes
idTips.description: Club-shaped capsules on very short stalks emerge from cushion centers, turning from green to reddish-brown when mature

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Tiny, overlapping leaves that curl and twist when dry, creating a crispy texture, but become plump and green when moist

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Changes dramatically from grayish-green when dry to bright green when wet, with older parts sometimes showing brownish tones

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Almost exclusively found on tree bark, especially favoring the rough bark of older deciduous trees like maples and oaks

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Cushions feel firm and slightly rough when dry, becoming soft and velvety when saturated with moisture

habitat: Club Pincushion grows exclusively on tree bark throughout New England's forests, preferring the rough, furrowed bark of mature deciduous trees like sugar maples, oaks, and ash trees. You'll find it from sea level to moderate elevations, thriving in both dense woodlands and more open areas where trees receive good air circulation. It's particularly common in older forests where the bark has developed deep grooves and crevices.

seasonality.spring: Cushions turn bright green with frequent spring rains, and sporophytes begin developing as small green buds at cushion centers. This is when the moss looks most vibrant and plump.
seasonality.summer: Sporophytes mature into distinctive club-shaped capsules that turn reddish-brown. Cushions may appear grayish and contracted during dry spells but quickly green up after rain.
seasonality.fall: Mature capsules release spores and may persist on the cushions. The moss remains visible but often appears more brownish as it prepares for winter dormancy.
seasonality.winter: Cushions appear gray-brown and tightly contracted against the bark, but remain alive and will quickly respond to winter thaws by turning green again.

funFact: Club Pincushion moss can survive being completely dried out for months, shrinking to a crispy gray shell, then fully revive and turn bright green again within minutes of getting wet - a superpower that allows it to live in the harsh, exposed environment of tree bark where most plants would quickly die.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with Crisped Pincushion moss, but Club Pincushion has sporophytes on much shorter stalks that barely extend beyond the cushion, while Crisped Pincushion's capsules sit on longer stalks that clearly rise above the moss. Memory trick: Club Pincushion keeps its "clubs" close to home.
compareHints: Among the pincushion mosses, Club Pincushion is distinguished by its very short sporophyte stalks compared to Crisped Pincushion's longer ones. Hutchins' Pincushion is much rarer and typically found at higher elevations or on rocks rather than bark. The other Ulota species in our region are either extremely rare or have different capsule shapes and growth patterns.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its relatives in the Ulota genus, crisped pincushion shows the most dramatic leaf curling when dry—much more pronounced than Hutchins' pincushion or club pincushion.
Compared to Crisped Pincushion (Ulota crispa), Curly Ulota has more uniformly curled leaves and tends to form denser cushions.

Hutchins' Pincushion forms the tightest, most perfectly dome-shaped cushions of all the Ulota species in New England, while Crisped Pincushion spreads more loosely and Club Pincushion tends to grow in more elongated patches.
Compared to the more common crisped pincushion (Ulota crispa), Ulota intermedia forms smaller, more compact cushions and typically has shorter, less prominently curled leaves when dry.
